segments.title: BJ Armstrong on applied naval history and education
segments.summary: BJ Armstrong connects his US Navy career, Naval Academy teaching, historical research, and work on professional development in the wardroom.
segments.body: Armstrong introduces his path from search-and-rescue helicopter pilot to permanent military professor, museum director, and historian at the US Naval Academy. He explains how courses in American naval history and strategy help new officers understand the institution they have joined. At the senior level, his capstone students practice historical research by producing substantial primary-source papers on subjects for which they can find evidence. His books range from early American maritime raiding to collections of Mahan and Sims, while Developing the Naval Mind gives wardrooms practical ways to read, lead seminars, and discuss professional writing.

evidence.note: Armstrong describes his naval career, Naval Academy roles, teaching, books, and wardroom education project.

segments.title: Museum work teaches historians how public history functions
segments.summary: Armstrong explains how directing the US Naval Academy Museum changed his understanding of institutional priorities, audiences, and effective public history.
segments.body: Historians often work near museums, consult their collections, and know museum professionals without seeing how the institution operates from within. Armstrong says his year directing the US Naval Academy Museum exposed him to the team's priorities and the practical choices behind public interpretation. That experience matters because presenting history to visitors demands different judgments from writing for an academic readership. He expects the work in Preble Hall to make him a better historian even after a full-time director takes over.

evidence.note: Armstrong reflects on the museum team, institutional priorities, public history, and how directing Preble Hall is changing his historical practice.

segments.title: Applied history should produce better questions
segments.summary: Armstrong argues that naval professionals should use history to ask better questions of the present, not copy old answers as checklists.
segments.body: Mahan belonged to a particular nineteenth-century setting, so his prescriptions cannot simply be transferred to the present. Armstrong places this method in the applied-history tradition he learned in King's College London's War Studies department while acknowledging that history pursued for its own sake is also legitimate. He treats the past as a store of experience that sharpens judgment about contemporary choices. The useful payoff is not a promise that the same action will produce the same result, but a stronger grasp of context, alternatives, and the costs already learned in the past.

evidence.note: The speakers distinguish applied historical judgment from copying past decisions.

segments.title: What Mahan would recognize in China and sea blindness
segments.summary: Mahan would recognize the maritime rise of China and the persistent difficulty of making continental societies understand their dependence on the sea.
segments.body: Armstrong links China's economic and political rise to Mahan's writing about Asian power at the opening of the twentieth century. He also emphasizes sea blindness: oceans, trade, and maritime security remain out of sight for much of the public. He notes that island societies such as Britain and Japan may experience the sea differently from the continentally focused United States. Mahan would still find the problem familiar because his own public writing tried to persuade Americans to look outward.

evidence.note: Armstrong identifies China's rise and sea blindness as features Mahan would understand.

segments.title: Mahan separated technological change from strategic purpose
segments.summary: Mahan expected aviation, submarines, and wireless communications to transform tactics without necessarily overturning the strategic choices facing states.
segments.body: The discussion rejects the caricature of Mahan as simply hostile to new technology. Armstrong notes that Mahan anticipated wireless telegraphy allowing fleets to disperse and reconcentrate, an early description of networked naval operations. Mahan also wrote before operational art became the standard middle tier between tactics and strategy, so his own vocabulary framed the problem through tactics, grand tactics, and strategy. His distinction was between tactical effects, where technology could be dramatic, and the more durable strategic questions of concentration, maritime access, and national purpose.

evidence.note: The speakers discuss Mahan on aviation, submarines, wireless telegraphy, tactics, and strategy.

segments.title: Presentism and new labels can conceal older strategic ideas
segments.summary: The speakers warn that fashionable terminology and technological presentism can obscure important continuities in strategic thought.
segments.body: Armstrong and Clarke note that modern institutions reward new labels even when terms such as geostrategy or operational art may restate older ideas associated with grand strategy or grand tactics. That incentive can make inherited concepts appear obsolete before their substance has been tested. Clarke calls the related error presentism: assuming technological superiority makes the past strategically irrelevant. Their warning is not to reject new technology, but to ask whether the strategic problem is genuinely new or only newly named.

evidence.note: The speakers compare modern strategic labels with older concepts and define presentism as dismissing the past because technology has changed.

segments.title: Why Corbett is often easier to read than Mahan
segments.summary: The speakers separate strategic merit from prose style, explaining why students may grasp Corbett more quickly even when Mahan rewards patient reading.
segments.body: Mahan's long late-Victorian paragraphs can make his argument difficult to locate until a compressed passage suddenly reveals the point. Corbett's background as a barrister, reporter, and novelist gave him practice in several kinds of writing before he turned fully to history. Armstrong therefore expects a student to get more from a random ten-page sample of Corbett on a first reading without treating that accessibility as proof of greater strategic intelligence. This distinction helps teachers choose readings honestly and reminds learners that difficulty of prose is not the same thing as depth or value.

evidence.note: Armstrong and Clarke compare Mahan's Victorian prose with Corbett's experience as a barrister, reporter, and novelist and discuss first-read accessibility.

segments.title: Mahan and Corbett wrote for opposite naval problems
segments.summary: Mahan and Corbett often agree on strategy, but their backgrounds and audiences made them emphasize different parts of the same naval problem.
segments.body: Mahan addressed a small, continentally oriented US Navy and public that needed convincing that fleets and major battles mattered. Corbett wrote for a global maritime empire already steeped in Trafalgar and therefore stressed the many tasks beyond decisive battle. Their biographies reinforced the contrast: Mahan was a career naval officer who became a historian, while Corbett was a civilian barrister, reporter, and novelist before turning fully to history and strategy. Their apparent rivalry comes partly from reading introductory passages without their institutional context. Deeper comparison shows substantial agreement about naval and national strategy.

evidence.note: Armstrong compares the authors' careers, national settings, intended audiences, and shared strategic ideas.

segments.title: The continental United States that Mahan asked to look outward
segments.summary: Mahan's emphasis on fleets and decisive battle answered the needs of a small post-Civil War navy and a country reaching the end of its continental frontier.
segments.body: Armstrong places Mahan's writing against the US Navy's contraction from nearly six hundred Civil War vessels to a deployable force of about fifty-two ships. That navy was not organized to fight a major fleet action, while the country remained focused on continental expansion and protected its economy with high tariffs. In 1890, the year The Influence of Sea Power upon History appeared, the census no longer classified an American frontier and the Battle of Wounded Knee marked the violent close of an expansionist era. Mahan's call for the United States to look outward therefore joined arguments for overseas trade, fleet construction, and a new international role rather than offering an abstract doctrine detached from national circumstances.

evidence.note: Armstrong connects US Navy downsizing, the 1890 census and Wounded Knee, tariffs, overseas trade, and Mahan's outward-looking argument.

segments.title: Structured disagreement reveals where Mahan and Corbett agree
segments.summary: A deliberately adversarial seminar can lead students beyond the easy Mahan-versus-Corbett binary when it ends in close comparison of their arguments.
segments.body: Armstrong cites paired Proceedings articles that recommend opposite theorists for confronting China yet arrive at much the same strategic advice. Clarke describes assigning strong students to defend Mahan and Corbett while classmates help each side research its case. As the seminar develops, the competing teams discover that different language and starting points conceal large areas of agreement. The exercise shows how a simplified opposition can prompt close reading, provided the class ultimately moves beyond the false binary.

evidence.note: The speakers describe paired articles and a seminar exercise in which apparent Mahan-Corbett opposition gives way to recognition of shared ideas.

segments.title: How historians present a strong inference without claiming proof
segments.summary: Clarke uses an unresolved British carrier-design question to show how converging archival clues can support a careful hypothesis without becoming a documented fact.
segments.body: A scholarly book needs to protect later readers from mistaking a plausible reconstruction for a documented conclusion. Clarke contrasts that constraint with a spoken format in which he can identify the surviving clues, state his inference, and repeatedly mark what he cannot prove. His example concerns Cammell Laird and a Royal Navy claim of prior strike-carrier design experience before HMS Ark Royal, when an unfinished Admiral-class battlecruiser appears to be the only hull fitting the description. The point is methodological rather than a declaration that the conversion plan certainly existed: historians can make their reasoning visible while preserving the boundary between evidence and informed judgment.

evidence.note: Clarke explains how he presents caveated archival inference through the Cammell Laird, Admiral-class, and Ark Royal carrier-design example.

segments.title: Mahan as a modern public communicator
segments.summary: The speakers imagine Mahan embracing television, social media, and long-form podcasts to educate the public about maritime affairs.
segments.body: Mahan was comfortable acting as a visible commentator, unlike the more behind-the-scenes Corbett. Corbett's family wealth allowed him to influence Admiralty thinking without depending on public attention, while Mahan relied much more heavily on income from prolific paid writing. Armstrong suggests that modern media would therefore suit both Mahan's livelihood and his effort to reach the audience whose sea blindness he wanted to overcome. Long-form formats might fit his expansive style better than short television sound bites.

evidence.note: The discussion contrasts Corbett's private influence with Mahan's paid public writing and likely use of modern media.

segments.title: Mahan's religion complicates a simple account of his racial views
segments.summary: Armstrong pairs a direct acknowledgment of Mahan's racism with evidence of his Episcopal reform work and correspondence with Booker T. Washington.
segments.body: Mahan's life extended beyond naval strategy into sustained writing about the Episcopal Church, Anglicanism, and moral conduct. Armstrong plainly describes him as a racist shaped by a Southern family and the United States of the 1840s, but warns that a modern label alone can conceal historical complexity. In the early twentieth century Mahan also worked through an Episcopal organization concerned with racial equality and exchanged letters with Booker T. Washington about opportunity for African Americans. The passage offers a useful example of biography that neither excuses a historical figure's prejudice nor erases actions that complicate a one-dimensional portrait.

evidence.note: Armstrong discusses Mahan's church writing, racism, Episcopal reform involvement, and correspondence with Booker T. Washington.

segments.title: Why navies struggle to explain their value
segments.summary: Naval institutions often assume the public shares experiences and vocabulary that make maritime trade, ports, and undersea infrastructure seem self-evidently important.
segments.body: Clarke identifies James Cable, a career army officer and diplomat, as a leading late-twentieth-century British naval theorist whose communication skills developed outside naval service. Life at sea can make sailors forget how unfamiliar the maritime world is to citizens ashore. Passing through dense traffic at Gibraltar or Malacca can reorient a naval professional while also creating assumptions that the public shares the same experience and vocabulary. Armstrong uses post-pandemic port disruption and damage to Baltic undersea cables to show how economic and digital life depends on maritime systems, even when news coverage frames the events only as economics or geopolitics. Effective naval communication must connect strategic issues to groceries, prices, internet access, and other lived experience.

evidence.note: Clarke names James Cable as an outside communicator before Armstrong explains naval insularity through trade disruption, ports, and undersea cable security.

segments.title: Public-facing history and the future of the field
segments.summary: Clarke and Armstrong argue that historians must explain foundational material and build routes to audiences beyond specialists if naval history is to remain useful and sustainable.
segments.body: Academic incentives reward writing for readers who already know the literature, while public audiences need the connecting explanation that specialists may regard as basic. Both speakers describe maintaining separate but complementary lanes for specialist scholarship and accessible professional writing. They also compare academia's inward language to naval sea blindness: institutions can become skilled at talking among themselves while failing to explain their public value. With secure humanities posts shrinking, they see public media and direct audience support as part of keeping historical work sustainable rather than merely promoting specialist publications.

evidence.note: The speakers discuss writing for newcomers, academic incentives, public history, and sustainable media.

segments.title: Fleet Problem IX revealed both carrier power and vulnerability
segments.summary: The 1929 Fleet Problem IX demonstrated that a carrier could deliver a decisive surprise strike and then be destroyed when left without adequate protection.
segments.body: Washington Naval Treaty limits constrained battleship and cruiser construction, leaving aircraft carriers as an important field for experimentation, and the US Navy used its interwar Fleet Problems to test ideas developed through war gaming at Newport. Saratoga separated from the fleet with a single cruiser, launched a surprise mass strike that closed the simulated Panama Canal, and was then found and destroyed by the opposing force. Aviators saw the carrier's independent striking power, while surface officers saw an exposed and vulnerable ship. Armstrong treats both lessons as correct, making carrier warfare a continuing effort to balance offensive reach with protection and intelligent employment. He also leaves open that carriers may eventually become too vulnerable, just as ships of the line and battleships lost their former roles. The historical lesson supports adaptation, not platform immortality.

evidence.note: Armstrong connects treaty constraints, war gaming, and Fleet Problem IX before drawing its competing but compatible carrier lessons.

segments.title: Carrier endurance depends on logistics and adaptation
segments.summary: Carriers retain value because their air power can be replenished at sea, while their designs have repeatedly adapted to geography, damage tolerance, and changing aircraft.
segments.body: Clarke argues that sustained operations require more than counting missile cells: aviation weapons can be replenished and aircraft kept flying while surface combatants face harder problems reloading vertical-launch systems at sea. Replacing organic aviation would therefore require changes across the fleet's logistics rather than merely substituting a new hull. British armored carriers illustrate how design traded air-group size for the ability to remain operational far from home repair yards. The enduring requirement is useful organic aviation, not preservation of an unchanged World War II carrier design.

evidence.note: Clarke connects carrier utility to at-sea replenishment, air power, geography, and armored-carrier design.

segments.title: The carrier debate is also an air-wing and maintenance debate
segments.summary: A carrier cannot be assessed apart from its changing air wing, and its combat value disappears if maintenance and logistics cannot keep aircraft operational.
segments.body: Armstrong recalls a carrier debate whose participants agreed that the air wing, rather than the hull alone, may be the element most in need of change. He cautions that uncrewed naval aviation is not new, citing Argus as a 1939 drone-carrier precedent and the US Navy's QH-50 DASH anti-submarine helicopters on destroyers in the 1960s and 1970s. Captain Stan Fischer's study of carrier maintenance shifts attention from pilots and aircraft to the interwar system invented for keeping airframes flyable at sea. That system depends on maintainers, spare parts, and logistics as much as aircraft performance. A carrier's combat value therefore has to be judged through the air wing and its sustaining organization, not the hull alone.

evidence.note: Armstrong discusses carrier air wings, historical drones, and the maintenance system behind combat aviation.

segments.title: Historical research reveals how naval adaptation actually works
segments.summary: Armstrong urges reformers to investigate why a naval practice exists and which organizational and leadership mechanisms made earlier adaptation possible.
segments.body: Armstrong challenges self-described innovators to ask how the practice they want to change came into being and why its requirements took their current form. Carrier history can then reveal the mechanisms and leadership choices through which fleets adapted, not merely provide old procedures to copy. Fischer's research on the invention of carrier maintenance shows how an apparently technical outcome depended on organization, logistics, and people. This is applied history at its most useful: it gives present-day officers better questions about how change succeeds.

evidence.note: Armstrong asks innovators to investigate why current systems exist and uses carrier-maintenance history to illustrate mechanisms of adaptation.

segments.title: Langley's thousand questions as a model of naval innovation
segments.summary: Captain Joseph Reeves used an open list of operational questions aboard USS Langley to draw practical carrier innovations from the entire crew.
segments.body: Early carrier sailors had to invent deck handling, hangar use, maintenance, launch, and recovery routines because no settled system existed. Reeves displayed his 'thousand questions' so anyone aboard could propose an answer. Armstrong presents the method as a historical example of participatory innovation and a useful subject for officers seeking mechanisms of adaptation rather than fashionable labels. The value lies less in copying Langley's answers than in understanding how Reeves opened operational problem-solving to expertise across the ship.

evidence.note: Armstrong explains Reeves's open question list and the invention of carrier operating practices aboard Langley.

segments.title: Sloops, the Littoral Combat Ship, and forgotten design precedents
segments.summary: Interwar Royal Navy sloops offered a historical precedent for flexible modular small combatants, while the LCS speed requirement pulled the design toward an unsuitable carrier-escort task.
segments.body: Clarke compares descriptions of interwar sloops with the later Littoral Combat Ship: both sought inexpensive vessels whose crews could shift among minesweeping, anti-submarine, gunboat, and diplomatic duties. He argues that extreme speed reflected an added requirement to accompany carriers during rapid theater moves, a role poorly matched to a lightly armed small combatant. A flotilla of flexible ships can distribute tasks through a network, as convoys and hunter-killer groups did, but that is not the same as making one LCS a carrier's sole escort. The example shows why innovators should investigate how requirements arose and search history for closely related institutional problems.

evidence.note: Clarke compares sloop requirements, LCS modularity and speed, carrier escort, and networked flotilla operations.

segments.title: Shipboard constraints can create informal spaces for adaptation
segments.summary: Clarke argues that limited space and manpower at sea can bring ranks together to solve problems in ways less common in segmented shore organizations.
segments.body: Army installations can separate officers, noncommissioned officers, and enlisted personnel into distinct professional spaces. A ship has less room for that separation and cannot simply summon a specialist from another unit when an unexpected problem appears at sea. Messes and wardrooms can therefore become comparatively rank-informal places where the available crew pool knowledge and work out a solution. Clarke presents this enforced interdependence as one cultural mechanism behind naval adaptability, while not claiming that rank or formal responsibility disappears aboard ship.

evidence.note: Clarke compares segmented army spaces with rank-informal naval spaces and explains why crews at sea must solve problems with the people aboard.

segments.title: Naval history is not settled when the battles are known
segments.summary: Armstrong rejects the idea that naval history is complete once wars and battles are described, pointing instead to institutions, technology, tactics, education, culture, and leadership.
segments.body: The disappearance or repurposing of US academic chairs in naval history reflects a narrow belief that the field has already settled its major questions. Armstrong welcomes broader social and political history but argues that much remains between social history and battle narrative: how technology is created, tactics and operational art develop, personnel are educated, and service cultures change. He points to institutional histories of the US Marine Corps as examples of work that explains how a service's culture, leadership, and approach to innovation came into being. Clarke adds that naval problems cross tidy technological periods, as when modern destroyers encountered sailing vessels during the Second World War.

evidence.note: The speakers identify institutional, technological, cultural, and leadership questions beyond battle narratives.

segments.title: Sailing ships created modern wartime boarding problems
segments.summary: Second World War destroyer crews still encountered sailing supply and hospital ships, forcing them to improvise boarding methods across supposedly separate technological eras.
segments.body: Clarke uses Mediterranean sailing vessels to show why neat technological periods can mislead naval historians. Sail-powered craft still carried supplies during the Second World War, and a modern destroyer might have to inspect a vessel presented as a hospital ship without damaging it or fouling its rig. Traditional age-of-sail boarding practices could not simply be transferred to a steel destroyer, so the crew had to reason through an unfamiliar approach in real time. The discussion then distinguishes the Altmark incident's location inside a Norwegian fjord - internal waters rather than merely territorial waters - to underline how operational adaptation could also carry acute legal and diplomatic risk.

evidence.note: Clarke describes wartime sailing logistics, a destroyer's boarding problem, and the Altmark incident inside Norwegian internal waters.

segments.title: Leadership is a human activity, not a checklist
segments.summary: Armstrong argues that leadership cannot be reduced to fixed steps because officers must understand and motivate different people under changing conditions.
segments.body: Rickover's demand that Proceedings stop publishing leadership articles represents a checklist view that Armstrong considers fundamentally mistaken. Naval officers manage complex technology, but their central responsibility is still leading human beings whose motivations and responses differ. Armstrong says leaders can learn as much from poor examples as good ones, while even describing people as colleagues who work with a leader rather than for one signals an important attitude. Orders matter in combat, yet reliable obedience in crisis rests on respect and trust built during ordinary service rather than rank alone. This human responsibility is why technical officer education still needs history, the humanities, and social science.

evidence.note: Armstrong contrasts Rickover's checklist conception with the human and relational demands of military leadership.

segments.title: Mahan and Sims made trust the center of leadership
segments.summary: Mahan's Nelson and Sims's junior officer both succeed through balanced trust in themselves, their superiors, and their subordinates.
segments.body: Mahan's account of Nelson locates his strength in confidence in his own judgment paired with confidence in his officers. Sims reaches a similar idea from below the chain of command: mission command works when a superior states the objective, permits initiative, and earns the subordinate's trust in the commander's intent. Their perspectives meet in the need to balance trust up and down the hierarchy rather than treating confidence as a one-way demand. Nelson at Copenhagen illustrates the balance, because Sir Hyde Parker offered a withdrawal signal while trusting Nelson to disregard it if his local judgment demanded continued action. Armstrong cautions that applying the theory is hard because trust can be misplaced and leaders must decide how to respond when it fails.

evidence.note: Armstrong compares Mahan and Sims on trust, Nelson, junior initiative, mission command, and Copenhagen.

segments.title: Reading turns lived experience into professional judgment
segments.summary: Mahan and Sims distinguish the merely practical officer from the professional who supplements technical competence with study and vicarious experience.
segments.body: Experience in successive jobs is valuable but too narrow to prepare an officer for every future responsibility. Mahan and Sims call the officer who masters only today's technical task 'practical,' contrasting that competence with a professional obligation to prepare intellectually for higher responsibility. Reading gives access to thousands of years of other people's decisions, allowing leaders to rehearse problems before encountering them personally. Armstrong recommends a sustainable habit rather than an academic burden: even fifteen or twenty minutes a day can build a book a month. His dean reinforces the norm by visibly blocking reading time on his calendar, modeling intellectual fitness just as military culture models physical training.

evidence.note: Armstrong links historical reading, vicarious experience, professional officers, and modeled intellectual fitness.

segments.title: The schooner Experiment and the value of small warships
segments.summary: Armstrong uses the American schooner Experiment's Quasi-War service to introduce the recurring usefulness of small warships that major navies can undervalue.
segments.body: Armstrong points to the American schooner Experiment, which fought in the Quasi-War, as a compact case for studying small warships on their own terms. He says navies often look negatively at such vessels even though they can be highly useful. The example opens the following discussion of how smaller commands can give junior officers responsibility earlier in their careers.

evidence.note: Armstrong names the schooner Experiment and the Quasi-War while introducing the value of small ships and early command.

segments.title: Destroyers as a school for wartime command
segments.summary: Small interwar destroyers gave junior officers early command, multi-ship coordination, and whole-ship experience that helped produce many senior admirals in the Second World War.
segments.body: Clarke observes that destroyer officers appear disproportionately among senior Royal Navy and US Navy commanders in the Second World War. Commanding a small ship or flotilla forced relatively junior officers to coordinate multiple vessels and work across departments with compact crews. Limited manpower also made narrow specialization difficult, so officers learned alongside enlisted sailors and became familiar with the whole ship. Clarke's example of Philip Vian being taught to paint by a chief petty officer shows how that practical exposure could begin at junior rank. Those assignments tested judgment and trust earlier than service in a battleship's larger, more specialized organization could.

evidence.note: The speakers connect small destroyer crews and early flotilla command to later senior leadership.
